strengths: The paper develops a rigorous theoretical extension of projected Discrete Flow Matching to variable-length insertion-based generation, introducing learnable per-position hazard rates (via Kumaraswamy CDFs) that control generation order while provably preserving the terminal data distribution (Proposition 1 and its proof in App. D.1).

The Kumaraswamy parameterization is a clever choice enabling closed-form likelihoods and inverse-CDF sampling, which together with a REINFORCE leave-one-out estimator allows joint training of the generator and the auxiliary order-dynamics network with a single backward pass per example, avoiding costly trajectory simulation that limited prior insertion-order learning methods (Gu et al., 2019; Brantley et al., 2019).
The connection to FlexMDM is made precise (Remark 1: fixing a=b=1 recovers FlexMDM exactly), situating the contribution clearly relative to prior work.

Empirical results on star-graph traversal convincingly show that the learned order dynamics recover the locally optimal traversal order (Fig. 4, Fig. 5 correlation analysis), providing decent mechanistic evidence that the method does what it claims.

On de novo molecule generation, LFlexMDM improves validity and quality metrics over the FlexMDM baseline at matched sampling budgets (Fig. 7), and the appendix provides an extensive, transparent set of ablations (aux. network size, shared vs separate backbone, nucleus threshold) rather than cherry-picking a single configuration.

The appendix is unusually thorough, including full derivations, gradient estimator construction for two parameter sets, and a schedule regularization term to address a documented degeneracy issue, indicating attention to technical rigor and reproducibility.
weaknesses: A core practical finding undercuts the paper's central claim: jointly learning both insertion (bin) and unmasking (bum) target rates is unstable (Fig. 6/9), forcing the authors to freeze bum=1 in all subsequent experiments. This means the method's real contribution reduces to learnable insertion order only, which is a narrower result than the title/framing ('Learnable Order Dynamics') suggests, and the instability itself is not deeply diagnosed or resolved (only worked around).

The molecule generation gains are sensitive to the nucleus-sampling truncation threshold p, and the best quality/validity numbers for LFlexMDM depend on aggressively lowering p (0.2-0.5), which simultaneously reduces diversity and uniqueness substantially (e.g., Table 2: uniqueness drops from ~96% to ~79-87%). This is a real trade-off that is somewhat downplayed as a straightforward improvement in the main text, and it is unclear whether a fairer comparison (matching diversity/uniqueness across models) would still favor LFlexMDM.

The FlexMDM baseline with confidence-based decoding collapses dramatically in Table 2 (86.5% validity, 5.8% quality, 20% uniqueness), which is a suspiciously large drop; it raises the question whether the baseline was adequately tuned, and this comparison point may make LFlexMDM's relative improvement appear larger than it would be against a well-tuned baseline.

Experimental validation is limited to two domains (synthetic star-graph traversal and one molecule dataset/SAFE-GPT-style benchmark) with relatively small-scale models; there is no evaluation on text or other more realistic sequence domains where the motivating claims about insertion-based generation (arbitrary order, relative position dependencies) would be most impactful.

No direct empirical comparison to closely related alternative insertion-based models mentioned in related work (EditFlows, ILM) despite discussing them at length; the only baselines are FlexMDM and standard MDM/ARM.

The REINFORCE-based gradient estimator for phi, while using a leave-one-out baseline, is still a score-function estimator with potentially high variance; no variance diagnostics, ablation of estimator quality, or comparison to alternative (e.g., pathwise) estimators is provided.

No reporting of computational overhead (wall-clock time, memory) introduced by the auxiliary target-rate network relative to standard FlexMDM training, despite this being relevant to the claimed practical efficiency of the single-backward-pass training scheme.

The large number of hyperparameter configurations reported in the appendix (aux. network size, shared/separate backbone, multiple p values) without a clear single recommended configuration makes it hard to assess practical robustness and increases risk of results being sensitive to tuning choices not easily generalizable to new datasets.

The impact statement is essentially a boilerplate placeholder and does not meaningfully engage with any potential ethical or societal considerations of generative molecule design or sequence generation.

strengths: The paper provides a mathematically careful treatment of the problem: a generalization of projected discrete flow matching with Poisson-process/Kumaraswamy-based target rate parameterization is derived rigorously, including proofs that the constructed target rates generate the desired marginals (Proposition 1) and that projected rate matching upper-bounds a terminal KL/log-likelihood objective (Proposition 5).

The insight of representing per-position insertion/unmasking as a two-event Poisson race with precedence constraints, and showing that with the Kumaraswamy family one gets closed-form hazards/likelihoods enabling training with a single backward pass (via REINFORCE leave-one-out) rather than full trajectory simulation, is a genuinely useful technical contribution that distinguishes this work from prior order-learning approaches requiring simulation (Gu et al. 2019; Brantley et al. 2019).

On the synthetic star-graph traversal task, the paper demonstrates convincingly (Figure 4, Figure 5, correlation analysis) that the learned target rates induce the known locally-optimal generation order, giving a clear and interpretable validation of the core mechanism.

The molecule-generation experiments include fairly extensive ablations (aux. network size, nucleus sampling threshold, confidence-based decoding, shared vs separate backbone), and error bars are reported throughout.
weaknesses: The central claim of jointly learnable order dynamics is undercut by the paper's own findings: training with a fully trainable unmasking schedule (b_um) is shown to be highly unstable (Figure 6/9), and the authors resort to freezing b_um=1 for all subsequent experiments. This means the "learnable order dynamics" contribution in practice reduces to learning only the insertion rate, a considerably narrower and less novel claim than advertised in the abstract/intro.

The reported improvements on de novo molecule generation are mixed and arguably overstated. Gains in validity are marginal (e.g., 98.9%→99.8%), while uniqueness/diversity often drop substantially (uniqueness falls from ~96% to below 80-90% in many configurations) when quality improves, indicating a quality-diversity trade-off rather than a clear win; the abstract's claim of "significant improvement" is not well supported when diversity/uniqueness losses are weighed.

The comparison between LFlexMDM and FlexMDM in Table 2 appears asymmetric: LFlexMDM is swept over many nucleus-sampling thresholds p and auxiliary network sizes to find favorable operating points, while FlexMDM is only reported at (implicitly) p=1.0 with/without confidence, without an equivalent sweep. This raises concerns about whether the comparison is fair, since nucleus sampling alone is known to trade diversity for quality.

The shared-backbone variant, which would be the more practical/efficient implementation, substantially underperforms the separate-backbone version (e.g., Table 1 hard setting: 87.9% vs 34.2-69.7% exact match), implying the method's benefits rely on doubling model capacity via a separate auxiliary network—an important practical cost that is not clearly flagged as a limitation.

Empirical scope is narrow: only a synthetic graph-traversal task and a single small-molecule dataset are used; there is no evaluation on text/language benchmarks or other domains where insertion-based generation is motivated in the introduction, nor any comparison against the other insertion-based baselines discussed at length in Related Work (ILM, EditFlows), despite these being the most relevant competing methods.

No analysis is given of the variance or reliability of the REINFORCE leave-one-out estimator (n=2 samples) used for training ϕ, despite this being a potential source of the observed instability; no ablation isolates its effect from the parameterization choice.

For the molecule generation task, unlike the graph-traversal analysis, there is no inspection of what order is actually learned or whether it is chemically sensible, leaving the central "order learning" narrative unverified in the only real-world task studied.
The paper does not report compute/wall-clock comparisons between LFlexMDM (separate backbone) and FlexMDM, despite implying efficiency as a selling point of the single-backward-pass training scheme.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: learning generation order for insertion-based variable-length discrete flow/diffusion models, where the action space is much larger than that of fixed-length unmasking models.

The theoretical contribution is substantial and carefully worked out: a generalized 'projected DFM' framework with Dirac/degenerate decoders and side information (Appendix C), a clean characterization of target conditional rates via two CDFs (Proposition 1) with a full derivation, and a Kumaraswamy parameterization that admits closed-form hazard rates and (in the equal-shape-parameter case) closed-form likelihoods, enabling tractable joint training.

The training procedure is efficient: a single backward pass per example combining a pathwise gradient for the generator and a REINFORCE leave-one-out estimator for the auxiliary target-rate network, avoiding full trajectory simulation, with Proposition 5 providing a principled upper bound on the KL between terminal path measures that the loss minimizes.

The empirical study is carefully designed around a synthetic task (star graph traversal) with a known locally-optimal order, which allows direct, interpretable verification that the model learns the intended order (visualized trajectories, order-vs-distance correlation analysis in Figure 5), lending credibility to the mechanism rather than just reporting aggregate metrics.

The ablations on design choices (flexible vs. fixed unmasking rate, shared vs. separate backbone, confidence-based decoding, nucleus sampling threshold) are thorough and transparently report both successes and failure modes (e.g., training instability when both bin and bum are freely learned), which aids reproducibility and understanding of the method's practical boundary conditions.

Results on de novo molecule generation (a realistic downstream task) show consistent improvements in validity and quality over the FlexMDM baseline across sampling budgets and auxiliary network sizes, with reasonably extensive hyperparameter sweeps reported in the appendix (Table 7).
weaknesses: In the reported main experiments, bum is fixed to 1 rather than learned, meaning the 'jointly learnable order dynamics' claim is empirically realized mainly through the insertion rate, while unmasking order is only indirectly influenced via confidence-based decoding; this somewhat narrows the scope of the central claim relative to how it is advertised in the abstract/introduction.

The quality improvements on molecule generation are substantially obtained by tuning the nucleus sampling threshold p downward (trading diversity/uniqueness for quality/validity), making it harder to cleanly attribute gains specifically to the learned order dynamics versus the interaction with decoding hyperparameters; a controlled comparison at matched diversity would strengthen the causal claim.

The shared-backbone variant shows a large and only empirically-noted performance drop on the hard star-graph task (34.2% vs. 93.6% exact match), which is an important practical consideration for scaling the method, but the underlying cause is not analyzed in depth (e.g., whether it stems from gradient interference between the REINFORCE and pathwise objectives).

Evaluation is limited to two narrow domains (synthetic graph traversal and small-molecule SAFE strings); no experiments on natural language or other structured sequence domains are provided, leaving open how well the approach scales to larger vocabularies, longer sequences, or more complex dependency structures.

The REINFORCE-based gradient for the auxiliary target-rate network could introduce variance and extra tuning burden (e.g., regularization terms in Appendix D.5.2 needed to prevent degenerate schedules), but the paper does not report wall-clock/compute overhead comparisons against the FlexMDM baseline to substantiate the claimed training efficiency.

The main paper is dense and relies heavily on the appendix for essential derivations and even for understanding some notational conventions (e.g., Z vs Z̄, projected rates), which may hinder readability and reproducibility for readers who do not consult the ~25 pages of appendix.
